message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary as a BLACK BOX. The C++ library source is NOT available and you must NOT look for it.

Binary: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable
Invoke: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable '<word>'      (exactly one argument)
It prints exactly 20 lines to stdout, one per API call, in this fixed order (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  singularize(word)
  3  camelize(word)                       // default 2nd param
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  underscore(word)
  6  classify(word)
  7  tableize(word)
  8  humanize(word)
  9  titleize(word)
  10 dasherize(word)
  11 parameterize(word)
  12 parameterize("A " + word + " Test")
  13 upcase(word)
  14 downcase(word)
  15 capitalize(word)
  16 decapitalize(word)
  17 truncate(word, 5)
  18 demodulize("Test::" + word)
  19 to_string(isPlural(word))    -> "0"/"1"
  20 to_string(isSingular(word))  -> "0"/"1"

With no argument it prints nothing. With an empty argument it ABORTS (std::out_of_range from
basic_string::substr inside demodulize) printing nothing to stdout.

TOOLING TIPS
- Extract one line:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p'
- Show exact bytes:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p' | od -c
- Loop:  for w in a b c; do printf '%s -> ' "$w"; /workspace/dataset/test20_executable "$w" | sed -n '5p'; done
- Use $'...' bash quoting for control bytes / high bytes, e.g. $'a\tb', $'\xc3\xa9'.
- 'file' is unavailable; 'strings', 'od', 'sed', 'nl' work.
- The binary is fast; run HUNDREDS of probes. Be exhaustive, not economical.

GROUND RULES
- Every claim in your output MUST be backed by an observed probe you actually ran.
- Assume C locale: toupper/tolower/isalnum/isspace behave as ASCII-only; bytes >= 0x80 are
  unchanged by case ops and are NOT alnum. VERIFY this rather than assuming.
- Note operations are byte-based (std::string), not char-based. Test multi-byte UTF-8.
- Report the algorithm as precise pseudocode that a Rust programmer can transcribe with zero guessing,
  operating on BYTES.


YOUR ASSIGNMENT (camelize):
Characterize lines 3 and 4: camelize(word) and camelize(word, false).
Working hypothesis to verify or refute:
  result = ""; cap = false
  for each byte c: if c=='_' { cap = true } else if cap { push toupper(c); cap=false } else { push c }
  line 4 additionally uppercases result[0] (if non-empty); line 3 does not.
Test heavily: leading underscore "_ab", trailing underscore "ab_", double "a__b", only "_", "__",
underscore before digit "a_1b", before non-alpha "a_-b", before UTF-8 "a_\xc3\xa9x",
mixed case inputs, dashes, spaces, "::", already-camel input, single char, digits-only,
and whether line 3 EVER lowercases the first byte (try "Hello_world", "HELLO_WORLD", "_Hello").
Also determine what line 4 does when result is empty or starts with a non-letter.

Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

for i in $(seq 1 255); do
  [ $i -eq 10 ] && continue
  b=$(printf "$(printf '\\%03o' $i)")
  out=$(./test20_executable "a_${b}z" | sed -n '3p')
  # expected under hypothesis: 'a' + toupper(b) + 'z'
  exp=$(python3 -c "
import sys
i=$i
c=chr(i)
print('a'+(c.upper() if 97<=i<=122 else c)+'z',end='')
" 2>/dev/null)
  [ "$out" != "$exp" ] && printf 'MISMATCH %d out=%q exp=%q\n' $i "$out" "$exp"
done; echo SWEEPDONE

content.text: Probing complete — ~2,120 invocations, zero mismatches against the model.

apis.name: camelize(word)  [line 3, default 2nd param — lower-camel]
apis.pseudocode:
camelize_lower(input: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = []
    cap = false
    for c in input:                     # iterate raw bytes, no UTF-8 decoding
        if c == 0x5F ('_'):
            cap = true                  # underscore is CONSUMED, never emitted
                                        # (repeated underscores just keep cap = true)
        else if cap:
            out.push(ascii_toupper(c))  # only 'a'..'z' (0x61..0x7A) map to c-32; every
                                        # other byte (digits, punctuation, control,
                                        # 0x80..0xFF) is pushed unchanged
            cap = false
        else:
            out.push(c)
    return out

# NOTES CONFIRMED BY PROBE:
#  - cap starts FALSE, so the very first byte of the input is emitted verbatim
#    UNLESS the input begins with '_' (then the first surviving byte is uppercased).
#  - The first byte is NEVER lowercased. "Hello_world" -> "HelloWorld",
#    "HELLO_WORLD" -> "HELLOWORLD", "X_y_Z" -> "XYZ".
#  - A trailing '_' leaves cap = true with nothing following; it is simply dropped.
#  - No other separator is special: '-', ' ', '.', '/', ':', tab, high bytes all pass through.
#  - '/' is NOT converted to '::' (unlike Rails).
#  - An all-underscore input yields the empty string (no crash).
#  - No acronym table, no inflection rules, no locale involvement.

evidence.input: exhaustive sweep: single byte X, "_X", "X_" for every byte 0x01..0xFF except 0x0A (762 probes)
evidence.output: 0 mismatches vs model; only exceptions were X=':' inputs where the PROGRAM aborts in demodulize (line 18), producing no stdout at all

evidence.input: random fuzz, 450 strings over alphabet {_,a,b,Z,Q,1,9,-,space,.,/,tab,0xC3,0xA9,0xFF,0x01,~,+,%,0x80}, len 1-12
random fuzz, 400 strings of uniformly random bytes 0x01..0xFF (excluding 0x0A and ':'), len 1-40, 30% with leading '_', 30% with trailing '_'

edge_cases: Leading '_': "_ab" -> "Ab" — the underscore is dropped and the following byte IS uppercased even in the 'lower' variant, so line 3 and line 4 are IDENTICAL for any input whose first byte is '_'.
Trailing '_': "ab_" -> "ab" — dangling cap flag is discarded, no crash.
Consecutive underscores collapse: "a__b" -> "aB", "____x" -> "X".
All-underscore input ("_", "__", "___") -> empty string on BOTH lines 3 and 4; the program prints an empty line, no crash.
Underscore before a digit: "a_1b" -> "a1b" (digit unchanged, cap consumed by the digit — the following 'b' is NOT uppercased).
Underscore before punctuation: "a_-b" -> "a-b" ('-' consumes the cap flag; 'b' stays lowercase).

Underscore before a UTF-8 lead byte: "a_\xc3\xa9x" -> "a\xc3\xa9x". The cap is consumed by 0xC3 which toupper leaves alone, so the multi-byte char is neither uppercased nor corrupted. Byte-based, not char-based.
Bytes >= 0x80 are never modified (verified across the full 0x01..0xFF sweep) — confirms C-locale/ASCII-only toupper.

Line 3 NEVER lowercases anything: "Hello_world"->"HelloWorld", "HELLO_WORLD"->"HELLOWORLD", "HelloWorld"->"HelloWorld". It is purely 'remove underscores, uppercase the byte after each run of underscores'.
'/' is NOT translated to '::' (Rails does this): "foo_bar/baz_qux" -> "fooBar/bazQux".
Existing "::" passes through untouched: "Foo::Bar" -> "Foo::Bar".
No acronym/inflection table is consulted; output is a pure character transform.

Single-byte input ':' (and "_:") makes the whole program abort with std::out_of_range from demodulize (line 18) before stdout is flushed, so lines 3/4 are unobservable for those inputs — this is a line-18 property, not a camelize property.
Empty input aborts the program (demodulize) so camelize("") is not directly observable, but all-underscore inputs prove the empty-result path is handled without crashing.

apis.name: camelize(word, false)  [line 4 — upper-camel / PascalCase]
apis.pseudocode:
camelize_upper(input: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = camelize_lower(input)      # EXACTLY the same transform as line 3
    if out is not empty:
        out[0] = ascii_toupper(out[0])
    return out

# Equivalently (indistinguishable by any probe I ran): the same loop as line 3 but
# with cap initialized to TRUE instead of false. These are observationally identical
# because the first byte written to `out` is always the first non-'_' byte of input,
# and ascii_toupper is idempotent.
#
# NOTES CONFIRMED BY PROBE:
#  - It uppercases the FIRST BYTE ONLY, not the first letter and not a full
#    'capitalize'. "1abc" -> "1abc" (leading digit is left alone AND 'a' is NOT
#    promoted); "-a" -> "-a"; " a" -> " a"; "helloWorld" -> "HelloWorld"
#    (the rest of the string is NOT lowercased).
#  - Empty result (e.g. input "_", "__", "___") -> empty output, no crash,
#    no out-of-range access.
#  - Lines 3 and 4 differ in at most the single first byte; nothing else.

evidence.output: FooBar/bazQux  ('/' not a separator; only the very first byte is promoted)
\xc3\xa9x — leading high byte unchanged, 'x' NOT promoted
\xc3\xa9Abc (od: 303 251 A b c) — identical to line 3

evidence.input: exhaustive sweep: "a_" + byte + "z" for every byte 0x01..0xFF except 0x0A (254 probes)
exhaustive sweep: single byte X, "_X", "X_" (762 probes)
850 random-string fuzz probes (structured alphabet + uniform random bytes, len 1-40)

edge_cases: Empty result is handled safely: inputs "_", "__", "___" print an empty line for line 4 (no out_of_range, no UB) — so the implementation guards on !result.empty() (or uses an initial-cap flag, which is equivalent).
Result starting with a non-letter is left completely unchanged: "1abc"->"1abc", "-a"->"-a", "123"->"123", "\xff"->"\xff". It does NOT search forward for the first alphabetic byte.
It is NOT 'capitalize' (upper-first + lower-rest): "helloWorld" -> "HelloWorld", "HELLO_WORLD" -> "HELLOWORLD".
It touches exactly ONE byte, not one UTF-8 character: for input "\xc3\xa9x" the leading 0xC3 is untouched and the following 'x' is NOT promoted.
When the input begins with '_', lines 3 and 4 are byte-identical (the leading-underscore cap already uppercased the first surviving byte).
Semantics are inverted relative to Rails naming: the DEFAULT (line 3) is lower-camel, and passing `false` (line 4) gives upper-camel/Pascal. Verified: "hello" -> line3 "hello", line4 "Hello".

uncertainties: camelize("") is not directly observable: the harness aborts on empty input via std::out_of_range in demodulize (line 18) before stdout is flushed. All-underscore inputs ("_", "__", "___") do exercise the empty-result path and print empty lines for both 3 and 4, so the empty case is safe; I infer camelize("") == "" for both.

I could not distinguish 'build lower-camel then uppercase result[0]' from 'run the same loop with cap initialized to true' for line 4. They are provably observationally identical (the first byte pushed is always the first non-'_' input byte, and toupper is idempotent), so either transcription is correct.

Inputs containing ':' as the sole byte, or "_:" , abort the whole program in demodulize, so lines 3/4 were skipped for those in the sweeps. However multi-byte inputs containing ':' (e.g. "a::b", "Foo::Bar") were probed successfully and matched the model, so I have no reason to think ':' is special to camelize.

Input bytes 0x00 (NUL) and 0x0A (newline) could not be tested: NUL cannot be passed through argv, and newline would desynchronize the line-indexed stdout parsing. I assume 0x0A behaves like any other non-alpha byte (passed through, consumes a pending cap).
The C locale was assumed and verified empirically (bytes 0x80-0xFF and 0xC0-0xDF are never case-mapped across the full 254-byte sweep), but I did not test under a non-C LC_CTYPE.
